title: Day 73 · Week 10, Day 3 — Parents: your weight and your sleep — the four pounds of fatherhood, the partner effect that triples the odds of change, the father's BMI in the child's, sixty-two minutes against thirteen, and the hours below which you don't drive
summary: The father's own body as a lever in the household. Garfield's 20-year Add Health cohort (10,253 young men): becoming a resident father was linked to a 2.6% BMI rise, about 4.4 lb for a six-foot man, while non-fathers lost about 1.4 lb. Jackson, Steptoe & Wardle (JAMA Intern Med 2015, 3,722 couples): when one partner changed, the other was about three times as likely to lose weight (men 26% vs 10%), five times as likely to become active (67% vs 26%) and twelve times as likely to quit smoking (48% vs 8%) — and a newly changed partner beat a always-healthy one. Fleten's MoBa study of 29,216 families: father's and mother's BMI predicted the child's at age three equally (0.13 vs 0.12 per SD), pointing to genes and the household over the womb. Healthy Dads, Healthy Kids trials (−7.6 kg vs 0 at 6 months; −3.3 vs +0.1 kg in the community trial) as the case for father-framed change. Then sleep: the AASM/SRS ≥7-hour consensus; short sleep and obesity (OR 1.55, Cappuccio 2008); Richter's German panel showing mothers lose 62 minutes a night after a birth against fathers' 13, with neither recovered at six years; 46% of pregnant women sleeping poorly (Sedov 2018); moderate–severe sleep apnoea in ~10% of men aged 30–49 (Peppard 2013); and Tefft's crash odds by hours slept (1.3 at 6 h, 1.9 at 5, 2.9 at 4, 15.1 under 4).
action: Tonight, set a bedtime alarm seven and a half hours before your morning alarm and run it for seven nights, noting each morning how many hours you actually slept. Write the average on a page with your name at the back of the Day 61 pregnancy file; if it's under seven, change one thing. And ask your partner: 'Do I snore, and does it wake you?' — then believe the answer.
